title: Contronyms: words that mean their own opposite
description: To sanction can mean to approve or to punish. To cleave can mean to split apart or to cling tight. Meet the two-faced words of English.

body.heading: One word, two opposite jobs
paragraphs: A contronym (also called an auto-antonym) is a single word with two meanings that oppose each other. A meeting can be sanctioned, meaning approved — or a country can be sanctioned, meaning punished. Same word, opposite fortunes.

Cleave is the classic double agent: it means to split apart, as a cleaver splits wood, and also to cling tightly, as in old wedding vows. The two meanings come from two different Old English words that slowly merged into one spelling.

body.heading: More double agents
paragraphs: Dust can mean removing dust (dust the shelves) or adding it (dust the cake with sugar). Oversight is both careful supervision and a careless mistake. Left can mean departed (she left) or remaining (only two are left) — sometimes in the same conversation.

Context does all the rescue work. Nobody has ever dusted a bookshelf with icing sugar by accident, because the situation makes the meaning obvious. Language trusts its listeners more than its spelling.

body.heading: Try it: spot the two faces
paragraphs: Deal out contronyms — bolt, clip, fast, fine, seed, stone, weather — and challenge each player to use one word in two sentences with opposite meanings. “The horse bolted” versus “bolt the door” is a fine start.
Then invent a safety rule for writers: which of your sentences would confuse a reader if heard aloud with no context? Rewriting one of those is a small masterclass in clear English.

takeaway: Contronyms are words with two faces; only the sentence around them tells you which face is speaking.
